Cabart Collinearity

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Drag the triangle's corners and change the angle: three special points always fall on one straight line.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Move the angle slider and tick the boxes to show the triangles, points and circle.
45°
Look for the math

Stand an isosceles triangle on each side of a triangle. Lines from the corners to the three new tips meet in one point. Do it twice with angles a right angle apart, and that point, its partner and the centre of the nine-point circle turn out to be collinear — whatever shape the triangle has.

Two angles that fit together

The slider sets the base angle x of the outer triangles, from 0° to 95° (it starts at 45°, as in the applet). The inner triangles use x − 90°, the algebraic angle that puts them on the other side of each side. An apex angle is 180° − 2x, so 45° gives the right-angled Vecten triangles and 30° gives the 120° apex triangles the original page mentions in connection with Napoleon. At 0° or 90° the tips run off to infinity and the applet draws no new points; this page hides them in the same cases. Which side counts as "outer" flips if you wind the triangle the other way, so the algebraic angle changes sign with the winding.

A point from three cevians

Each triple of tips gives three cevians; they concur at a Kiepert point. With side lengths a = BC, b = CA, c = AB and corner angles A, B, C, its barycentric coordinates are

a / sin(A + x) : b / sin(B + x) : c / sin(C + x).

Equivalently, after clearing denominators, they are a[cos(B − C) − cos(B + C + 2x)] and its cyclic partners. The core builds the point the applet's way — rotate a side by x, intersect the rays, and average the three intersections — and the logic test checks both weight formulas against it on hundreds of triangles.

The centre of the nine-point circle

The centre N comes from the midpoints of the three sides: it is their circumcenter, and the circle through all six notable points is the nine-point circle. In barycentrics N is a cos(B − C) : b cos(C − A) : c cos(A − B). The applet uses the mean of its distances to the three midpoints as the radius; the test confirms that this is the same point as the barycentric formula.

Why the three points line up

Write y = x − 90°. Because cos(B + C + 2y) = −cos(B + C + 2x), the sums of the two sets of weights obey s₁ + s₂ = 2s₃, where s₃ is the sum of N's weights. Then

2 s₃ · N = s₁ · K(x) + s₂ · K(y),

so N is a weighted centre of the two Kiepert points and must lie on their line. The test measures the cross product of the three points over more than 600 configurations: it stays below 1e-9 board units after scaling.

Try 45° with both boxes ticked: those are the Vecten points. Then nudge one corner — the three dots keep sharing a line.
